roots-1: The backup job is a cron-scheduled script on a single host that wraps a database dump tool.
Existing monitoring only reacts to errors the job itself reports, with no check for a missing run.
No team is formally assigned to own backups or run periodic restore drills.
1.why.1: The job is a shell wrapper launched by cron on a single Linux host, with its own lock file and a permitted start-time window.
Cron mails the ops inbox on non-zero exits or output, and the crontab entry redirects the wrapper's output.
The lock file is a plain file created by the script, not a kernel-held flock.
1.why.2: The backup job is a shell script scheduled from cron on the database host rather than from a central job scheduler.
Existing alerting matches error lines or non-zero exits in shipped logs and has no rule that evaluates missing events.
The database team owns the backup job while a separate platform or SRE team owns the monitoring stack and on-call paging.
1.why.3: The backup job is a cron entry on the database host, originally set up by one engineer rather than a team.
No staging or scratch environment large enough to hold a full production restore currently exists.
The organization has no compliance or audit requirement that demands evidence of successful restores.
Backup files are encrypted, with keys and production credentials controlled by a separate security team.

inputs.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.

answers.answer: The wrapper script exits 0 on a stale lock file or missed cron window, so skipped runs look like successes.
The author coded the lock-held and outside-window branches as deliberate exit 0 no-ops to stop cron from mailing on expected overlaps.
Early versions exited non-zero when a long dump overran the next slot, flooding the ops inbox with cron mail until someone silenced it.
The start-window guard was added quickly to keep dumps off daytime production load and copied the lock branch's existing exit 0.
The wrapper was reviewed as a small shell utility, so no reviewer questioned what each guard branch's exit status told the scheduler.
The lock is a bare file with no PID or age check, so a crashed run's leftover lock looks identical to a live run.
The script creates the lock with touch instead of flock, so the kernel never releases it when the owning process dies.
OOM kills and host reboots during a dump bypass the script's trap cleanup, leaving the lock file behind for every later night.
The lock sits on persistent disk beside the backup directory rather than on tmpfs, so a reboot does not clear it.
The wrapper's exit contract has only success and failure, with no distinct skipped status that cron or a dashboard could recognise.
The script decides its exit code from guard branches alone and never checks whether a new, non-empty dump file was written tonight.
The crontab redirects the wrapper's output to /dev/null, so even its 'lock held, skipping' log line reaches nobody.
Cron's only signal is the exit status, and the wrapper was written for that binary view before any skip paths existed.
Alerting fires only on errors the job emits, so a run that never starts sends no signal and no expected-heartbeat check exists.
Backup monitoring was built as error-log scraping when the script was written, and no dead-man's-switch service was ever provisioned alongside it.
The script's only reporting path is cron mailing stderr to an ops alias, which feeds the error filter and nothing else.
The monitoring stack offers only pattern and threshold rules on arriving events, so an absence-of-run rule cannot even be expressed.
The job was added hastily during initial database provisioning and skipped the readiness review that would have demanded a success signal.
After noisy backup pages, the team deliberately narrowed alert rules to hard errors, and a heartbeat check was seen as reintroducing noise.
Planned maintenance windows repeatedly paged on-call for expected backup interruptions, prompting the rules to be trimmed to fatal errors only.
A heartbeat would need maintenance-window silences, and nobody wanted to keep a suppression calendar for the database host current.
On-call health is measured by page count, so any check that could add pages lacked a sponsor willing to propose it.
The schedule lives only in one host's crontab, so monitoring holds no record of which nightly runs are expected.
The job predates the team's adoption of a scheduler with run history, and migrating legacy cron jobs was deprioritized as already working.
The database team owns the crontab while the platform team owns alerting, and neither backlog includes wiring expected-run checks between them.
No inventory of scheduled jobs exists, so reviews of monitoring coverage never list the backup job as needing a heartbeat.
No one owns scheduled restore drills, so backup files are never opened or counted until an actual outage forces a restore.
The backup cron was set up by one engineer, and ownership never passed to a team when that engineer moved on.
The cron entry lives on the database host outside the service catalogue, so no owner field existed to reassign.
The offboarding checklist covers access revocation but not handing over scheduled jobs, so the backup cron was never reviewed.
DBA and platform teams each assume the other covers backups, since the job spans database dumps and host storage.
Restore drills appear in no team's sprint goals or on-call runbook, so they lose every scheduling contest against feature work.
Teams are measured on shipped features and uptime, and a passing drill produces no metric anyone reports upward.
No audit or customer contract demands proof of recoverability, so nobody outside engineering ever asks for drill results.
Past ad hoc restores happened to find a recent file, so the team treats drills as redundant rather than protective.
No environment exists that can hold a full restore, so each drill would first need infrastructure nobody has budgeted.
The database outgrew the old staging server's disk gradually, so no single moment prompted a request for a larger instance.
Per-team cloud spend caps mean a temporary full-size restore instance would breach the platform team's monthly budget.
Restoring needs encryption keys and production credentials held by security, whose access requests take days for each drill.
